rally-4.history: The feature ranks at the 69.6th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-4.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.059 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-4.portfolio: A deep reading can raise mean-reversion potential, but should be read with crash risk.
rally-4.example: It measures shorter-horizon damage and oversold conditions.

rally-5.title: Cross-asset breadth
rally-5.measure: The share of the 24 assets trading above their own 20-day moving averages.

structure-overview.title: Structural health
structure-overview.measure: Whether the 24 instruments are still behaving like genuinely different investments, or are being controlled by the same macro force.
structure-overview.current: The current Composite · all estimators view is summarised by four plain-language cards.
structure-overview.effect: Raises or lowers the fragility warning, but does not by itself forecast a market decline.
structure-overview.portfolio: Treat the book as more concentrated than the ticker count suggests when several measures deteriorate together.
structure-overview.example: Owning SPY, QQQ, XLK, XLY, EFA, and HYG can look like six positions but behave like one broad risk-on trade.

struct-ar1.title: One factor controls the market
struct-ar1.technical: Absorption ratio AR1 / first eigenvalue share
struct-ar1.measure: The share of all cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
struct-ar1.current: 44.6% of total movement is explained by one factor.
struct-ar1.effect: A rising reading increases fragility because more assets answer to the same market “conductor.”
struct-ar1.portfolio: Expect diversification to work less well if a shock hits the dominant factor.
struct-ar1.example: During a liquidity shock, technology, banks, small caps, high yield, and overseas equities may all become the same trade.

struct-erank.title: 24 assets behave like fewer bets
struct-erank.measure: An estimate of how many independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
struct-erank.effect: A falling effective rank raises structural risk.
struct-erank.portfolio: Position count may overstate diversification. Size the book as if it contained roughly this number of independent bets.
struct-erank.example: SPY, QQQ, XLK, and XLY may all belong to one US growth cluster rather than four separate ideas.

struct-links.title: Strongly connected asset pairs
struct-links.measure: How many of the 276 unique asset pairs have a correlation strong enough to pass the selected threshold.
struct-links.current: 32 of 276 pairs are currently classified as strong links.
struct-links.history: That equals 12% of all possible pairs.
struct-links.effect: More links mean a shock can travel through more parts of the portfolio.
struct-links.portfolio: Look for duplicate exposures and avoid assuming that different tickers imply different risk.
struct-links.example: If SPY–QQQ, QQQ–XLK, and SPY–XLK are all strong links, the three form one crowded cluster.

struct-speed.title: Speed of deterioration
struct-speed.measure: How quickly the share of strong cross-asset relationships is changing.
struct-speed.current: Strong-link density changed -1.8 percentage points in 20 trading days.
struct-speed.history: The speed of change can be more informative than a permanently high but stable level.
struct-speed.effect: Rapid deterioration strengthens the warning because the market structure is changing now.
struct-speed.portfolio: Raise monitoring frequency and reduce marginal risk before the headline index necessarily breaks.
struct-speed.example: A market can remain near its high while correlations underneath the surface rise sharply.

advanced-ar3.title: Top three factors share
advanced-ar3.measure: The percentage of total cross-asset movement explained by the three largest common factors.
advanced-ar3.current: The top three factors explain 68.6% of movement.
advanced-ar3.effect: Raises structural concentration when it climbs.
advanced-ar3.portfolio: A portfolio may be exposed mainly to three macro drivers such as risk appetite, rates, and the US dollar.
advanced-ar3.example: Twenty-four assets can still be mostly controlled by only three broad forces.

advanced-gap.title: Dominant factor ratio
advanced-gap.technical: Spectral gap: first eigenvalue divided by second eigenvalue
advanced-gap.measure: How much stronger the largest common factor is than the second-largest factor.
advanced-gap.current: The first factor is approximately 2.6× as strong as the second.
advanced-gap.effect: Supports a herding or one-factor-market warning.
advanced-gap.portfolio: If the dominant factor reverses, many apparently unrelated positions can move together.
advanced-gap.example: A single “rates higher” trade can dominate utilities, REITs, technology, bonds, and the dollar.

advanced-cluster.title: Cluster tightness
advanced-cluster.measure: How often strongly linked assets form closed groups in which each member is connected to the others.
advanced-cluster.effect: Can raise crash risk when crowded groups become tightly synchronized.
advanced-cluster.portfolio: A cluster can amplify contagion because weakness in one member is confirmed by the others.
advanced-cluster.example: SPY, QQQ, and XLK all strongly linked to one another form a closed triangle.

advanced-condition.title: Matrix instability
advanced-condition.technical: Condition number of the correlation matrix
advanced-condition.measure: How unbalanced the correlation matrix is between its strongest and weakest risk directions.
advanced-condition.effect: Raises concern about fragile covariance estimates rather than directly forecasting price direction.
advanced-condition.portfolio: Do not trust precise optimizer weights when the matrix is unstable; use constraints and robustness checks.
advanced-condition.example: Like a table carrying most of its weight on one leg, a small disturbance can change the balance.

advanced-mp.title: Common factor above random noise
advanced-mp.measure: Whether the dominant eigenvalue is larger than what random statistical noise could plausibly generate.
advanced-mp.current: The excess is 8.6 above the random-noise boundary.
advanced-mp.effect: Confirms whether the common market structure is likely real rather than accidental correlation.
advanced-mp.portfolio: Treat the dominant factor as economically meaningful while still testing stability out of sample.
advanced-mp.example: It asks whether the “one market conductor” is real or just a pattern created by chance.

asset-avg-relationship.title: Average relationship
asset-avg-relationship.measure: The average strength of one asset’s relationship with the other 23 assets. Positive and negative signs are both counted as strong dependence.
asset-avg-relationship.current: The table shows the raw value and a Low / Medium / High label.
asset-avg-relationship.history: A rising average means the asset is becoming less independent.
asset-avg-relationship.effect: This is a dependence measure, not a buy or sell signal.
asset-avg-relationship.portfolio: High average relationship means the asset may duplicate risks already present elsewhere in the book.
asset-avg-relationship.example: An average of 0.56 means the asset is fairly connected to the broader universe.

asset-strong-links.title: Strong links
asset-strong-links.technical: Network degree at the selected threshold
asset-strong-links.measure: The number of other assets whose correlation passes 0.70 under the current edge setting.
asset-strong-links.current: The table reports a count out of 23 possible relationships.
asset-strong-links.history: A rising count means the asset is moving toward the centre of the market network.
asset-strong-links.effect: High connectivity can confirm broad contagion or duplicate beta.
asset-strong-links.portfolio: Owning multiple highly connected hubs may not add diversification.
asset-strong-links.example: 18 / 23 means the asset has strong relationships with eighteen other instruments.

asset-strongest-link.title: Strongest relationship
asset-strongest-link.measure: The single asset with the strongest current relationship to the selected ticker.
asset-strongest-link.current: The sign is retained: positive means they move together; negative means they tend to move opposite.
asset-strongest-link.history: Relationships can change across macro regimes.
asset-strongest-link.effect: Useful for identifying duplicate exposure or a possible offset.
asset-strongest-link.portfolio: Validate whether the relationship is stable before treating it as a hedge.
asset-strongest-link.example: QQQ +0.85 with XLK suggests the two positions may duplicate US growth risk.

asset-vs-spy.title: Relationship to SPY
asset-vs-spy.measure: How closely the asset currently moves with the broad US equity market.
asset-vs-spy.current: Positive values imply equity-like co-movement; negative values may indicate an offset.
asset-vs-spy.history: The sign and magnitude can change between growth, inflation, and liquidity shocks.
asset-vs-spy.effect: Helps classify the asset’s current portfolio role.
asset-vs-spy.portfolio: A low or negative SPY correlation can diversify equity beta, but only if it persists when stress rises.
asset-vs-spy.example: TLT may offset SPY in a growth shock but fail during an inflation shock.

asset-corr-change.title: 20-day change in relationship
asset-corr-change.measure: Whether the asset is becoming more or less connected to the rest of the universe.
asset-corr-change.current: Positive values mean dependence has increased during the last 20 sessions.
asset-corr-change.history: A rapid increase is often more informative than a stable high level.
asset-corr-change.effect: Supports or weakens the current fragility warning.
asset-corr-change.portfolio: A previously independent hedge becoming highly correlated can leave the portfolio unexpectedly exposed.
asset-corr-change.example: Gold can stop diversifying if dollar or real-yield stress starts controlling both gold and equities.

driver-overview.title: Model driver contributions
driver-overview.measure: Which variables are currently pushing the rally or crash score higher or lower.
driver-overview.current: Red positive values increase that score; green negative values reduce it.
driver-overview.history: The numbers are relative contributions on the ORCA-Lite scale, not probabilities.
driver-overview.effect: Explains the current ranking but does not prove the variable caused the market move.
driver-overview.portfolio: Use the driver mix to distinguish structural risk from an oversold or volatility-driven signal.
driver-overview.example: A crash warning driven by rising network density is different from one driven only by a one-day volatility spike.

driver-spectral-share.title: Spectral / graph share
driver-spectral-share.technical: Share of absolute model contribution from correlation-network features
driver-spectral-share.measure: How much of the score explanation comes from eigenvalue, correlation, and graph-topology features rather than price indicators.
driver-spectral-share.history: The ORCA paper emphasises structural features for crash detection.
driver-spectral-share.effect: A high share means the warning is mainly about market structure.
driver-spectral-share.portfolio: Structural warnings may appear before headline volatility fully reacts.
driver-spectral-share.example: The crash score rises because diversification is collapsing even while the index remains near its high.

outcome-performance.title: Performance by regime
outcome-performance.technical: Event-based forward return and drawdown analysis
outcome-performance.measure: What the selected index did after the first day of each historical regime episode.
outcome-performance.current: The table summarises 10-day outcomes for the selected index and time window.
outcome-performance.history: Episodes—not every daily observation—are counted to reduce repeated labels from the same event.
outcome-performance.effect: This is a validation tool, not an input to the current signal.
outcome-performance.portfolio: A useful regime should show economically different forward outcomes after costs and without look-ahead leakage.
outcome-performance.example: If Crisis episodes do not have worse forward drawdowns than Normal episodes, the regime map has little practical value.

crash-0.title: 20-day realised volatility
crash-0.measure: The annualised variability of daily SPY returns over the last 20 trading days.
crash-0.history: The feature ranks at the 11.7th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-0.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.115 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-0.portfolio: It can confirm stress, but it often reacts after fragility has already increased.
crash-0.example: Higher realised volatility means the market is making larger daily moves than usual.

crash-1.title: Clustering coefficient
crash-1.measure: How often strongly linked assets form tightly connected groups or triangles.
crash-1.history: The feature ranks at the 73.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-1.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.046 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-1.portfolio: Dense clusters can reveal duplicate exposures that look diversified only because they use different tickers.
crash-1.example: If SPY links to QQQ and XLK, and QQQ also links to XLK, they form a tight cluster.

crash-2.title: Price versus 50-day moving average
crash-2.measure: The percentage distance between SPY and its 50-day average price.
crash-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-2.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.044 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-2.portfolio: Below-trend prices can confirm weakness or create rebound potential depending on the wider regime.
crash-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

crash-3.title: 60-day drawdown
crash-3.measure: How far SPY is below its highest close in the last 60 trading days.
crash-3.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-3.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.040 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-3.portfolio: A deep drawdown can create rebound potential while also indicating an unstable market.
crash-3.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

crash-4.title: One-factor absorption ratio (AR1)
crash-4.measure: The share of total cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
crash-4.history: The feature ranks at the 47.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-4.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.010 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-4.portfolio: A high or rapidly rising value means diversification is becoming more dependent on one macro driver.
crash-4.example: If AR1 is 40%, one broad force—such as liquidity, rates, inflation, or fear—explains about 40% of the movement across all 24 assets.

crash-5.title: Effective rank / effective bets
crash-5.measure: An estimate of how many statistically independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
crash-5.history: The feature ranks at the 49.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-5.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.002 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-5.portfolio: A falling value warns that the number of holdings may overstate actual diversification.
crash-5.example: A reading of 8 means 24 tickers currently behave more like eight genuinely different bets.

crash-6.title: Strong-connection share (edge density)
crash-6.measure: The fraction of all 276 unique asset pairs with absolute correlation above 0.50.
crash-6.history: The feature ranks at the 50.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-6.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.000 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-6.portfolio: A high or rising value means shocks can spread across more of the portfolio.
crash-6.example: A reading of 46% means roughly 127 of 276 pairs have a strong relationship.

rally-0.title: Five-day return / short-term reversal
rally-0.measure: SPY's total return over the last five trading days.
rally-0.history: The feature ranks at the 20.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-0.effect: It currently reduces the rally score by -0.120 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-0.portfolio: The signal is more credible when breadth and credit also improve.
rally-0.example: A positive rebound after a drawdown may strengthen a rally setup.

rally-1.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-1.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.100 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-1.portfolio: A deep drawdown can create rebound potential while also indicating an unstable market.
rally-1.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

rally-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-2.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.088 on the ORCA-Lite scale.

rally-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

rally-3.title: 20-day realised volatility

rally-3.history: The feature ranks at the 14.7th percentile in its comparison history.

rally-4.title: 20-day drawdown

rally-4.history: The feature ranks at the 69.6th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-4.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.059 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-4.portfolio: A deep reading can raise mean-reversion potential, but should be read with crash risk.
rally-4.example: It measures shorter-horizon damage and oversold conditions.

rally-5.title: Cross-asset breadth
rally-5.measure: The share of the 24 assets trading above their own 20-day moving averages.

structure-overview.title: Structural health
structure-overview.measure: Whether the 24 instruments are still behaving like genuinely different investments, or are being controlled by the same macro force.
structure-overview.current: The current EWM · 30D half-life view is summarised by four plain-language cards.
structure-overview.effect: Raises or lowers the fragility warning, but does not by itself forecast a market decline.
structure-overview.portfolio: Treat the book as more concentrated than the ticker count suggests when several measures deteriorate together.
structure-overview.example: Owning SPY, QQQ, XLK, XLY, EFA, and HYG can look like six positions but behave like one broad risk-on trade.

struct-ar1.title: One factor controls the market
struct-ar1.technical: Absorption ratio AR1 / first eigenvalue share
struct-ar1.measure: The share of all cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
struct-ar1.current: 45.2% of total movement is explained by one factor.
struct-ar1.effect: A rising reading increases fragility because more assets answer to the same market “conductor.”
struct-ar1.portfolio: Expect diversification to work less well if a shock hits the dominant factor.
struct-ar1.example: During a liquidity shock, technology, banks, small caps, high yield, and overseas equities may all become the same trade.

struct-erank.title: 24 assets behave like fewer bets
struct-erank.measure: An estimate of how many independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
struct-erank.effect: A falling effective rank raises structural risk.
struct-erank.portfolio: Position count may overstate diversification. Size the book as if it contained roughly this number of independent bets.
struct-erank.example: SPY, QQQ, XLK, and XLY may all belong to one US growth cluster rather than four separate ideas.

struct-links.title: Strongly connected asset pairs
struct-links.measure: How many of the 276 unique asset pairs have a correlation strong enough to pass the selected threshold.
struct-links.current: 184 of 276 pairs are currently classified as strong links.
struct-links.history: That equals 67% of all possible pairs.
struct-links.effect: More links mean a shock can travel through more parts of the portfolio.
struct-links.portfolio: Look for duplicate exposures and avoid assuming that different tickers imply different risk.
struct-links.example: If SPY–QQQ, QQQ–XLK, and SPY–XLK are all strong links, the three form one crowded cluster.

struct-speed.title: Speed of deterioration
struct-speed.measure: How quickly the share of strong cross-asset relationships is changing.
struct-speed.current: Strong-link density changed +2.9 percentage points in 20 trading days.
struct-speed.history: The speed of change can be more informative than a permanently high but stable level.
struct-speed.effect: Rapid deterioration strengthens the warning because the market structure is changing now.
struct-speed.portfolio: Raise monitoring frequency and reduce marginal risk before the headline index necessarily breaks.
struct-speed.example: A market can remain near its high while correlations underneath the surface rise sharply.

advanced-ar3.title: Top three factors share
advanced-ar3.measure: The percentage of total cross-asset movement explained by the three largest common factors.
advanced-ar3.current: The top three factors explain 68.3% of movement.
advanced-ar3.effect: Raises structural concentration when it climbs.
advanced-ar3.portfolio: A portfolio may be exposed mainly to three macro drivers such as risk appetite, rates, and the US dollar.
advanced-ar3.example: Twenty-four assets can still be mostly controlled by only three broad forces.

advanced-gap.title: Dominant factor ratio
advanced-gap.technical: Spectral gap: first eigenvalue divided by second eigenvalue
advanced-gap.measure: How much stronger the largest common factor is than the second-largest factor.
advanced-gap.current: The first factor is approximately 2.8× as strong as the second.
advanced-gap.effect: Supports a herding or one-factor-market warning.
advanced-gap.portfolio: If the dominant factor reverses, many apparently unrelated positions can move together.
advanced-gap.example: A single “rates higher” trade can dominate utilities, REITs, technology, bonds, and the dollar.

advanced-cluster.title: Cluster tightness
advanced-cluster.measure: How often strongly linked assets form closed groups in which each member is connected to the others.
advanced-cluster.effect: Can raise crash risk when crowded groups become tightly synchronized.
advanced-cluster.portfolio: A cluster can amplify contagion because weakness in one member is confirmed by the others.
advanced-cluster.example: SPY, QQQ, and XLK all strongly linked to one another form a closed triangle.

advanced-condition.title: Matrix instability
advanced-condition.technical: Condition number of the correlation matrix
advanced-condition.measure: How unbalanced the correlation matrix is between its strongest and weakest risk directions.
advanced-condition.effect: Raises concern about fragile covariance estimates rather than directly forecasting price direction.
advanced-condition.portfolio: Do not trust precise optimizer weights when the matrix is unstable; use constraints and robustness checks.
advanced-condition.example: Like a table carrying most of its weight on one leg, a small disturbance can change the balance.

advanced-mp.title: Common factor above random noise
advanced-mp.measure: Whether the dominant eigenvalue is larger than what random statistical noise could plausibly generate.
advanced-mp.current: The excess is 9.1 above the random-noise boundary.
advanced-mp.effect: Confirms whether the common market structure is likely real rather than accidental correlation.
advanced-mp.portfolio: Treat the dominant factor as economically meaningful while still testing stability out of sample.
advanced-mp.example: It asks whether the “one market conductor” is real or just a pattern created by chance.

asset-avg-relationship.title: Average relationship
asset-avg-relationship.measure: The average strength of one asset’s relationship with the other 23 assets. Positive and negative signs are both counted as strong dependence.
asset-avg-relationship.current: The table shows the raw value and a Low / Medium / High label.
asset-avg-relationship.history: A rising average means the asset is becoming less independent.
asset-avg-relationship.effect: This is a dependence measure, not a buy or sell signal.
asset-avg-relationship.portfolio: High average relationship means the asset may duplicate risks already present elsewhere in the book.
asset-avg-relationship.example: An average of 0.56 means the asset is fairly connected to the broader universe.

asset-strong-links.title: Strong links
asset-strong-links.technical: Network degree at the selected threshold
asset-strong-links.measure: The number of other assets whose correlation passes 0.30 under the current edge setting.
asset-strong-links.current: The table reports a count out of 23 possible relationships.
asset-strong-links.history: A rising count means the asset is moving toward the centre of the market network.
asset-strong-links.effect: High connectivity can confirm broad contagion or duplicate beta.
asset-strong-links.portfolio: Owning multiple highly connected hubs may not add diversification.
asset-strong-links.example: 18 / 23 means the asset has strong relationships with eighteen other instruments.

asset-strongest-link.title: Strongest relationship
asset-strongest-link.measure: The single asset with the strongest current relationship to the selected ticker.
asset-strongest-link.current: The sign is retained: positive means they move together; negative means they tend to move opposite.
asset-strongest-link.history: Relationships can change across macro regimes.
asset-strongest-link.effect: Useful for identifying duplicate exposure or a possible offset.
asset-strongest-link.portfolio: Validate whether the relationship is stable before treating it as a hedge.
asset-strongest-link.example: QQQ +0.85 with XLK suggests the two positions may duplicate US growth risk.

asset-vs-spy.title: Relationship to SPY
asset-vs-spy.measure: How closely the asset currently moves with the broad US equity market.
asset-vs-spy.current: Positive values imply equity-like co-movement; negative values may indicate an offset.
asset-vs-spy.history: The sign and magnitude can change between growth, inflation, and liquidity shocks.
asset-vs-spy.effect: Helps classify the asset’s current portfolio role.
asset-vs-spy.portfolio: A low or negative SPY correlation can diversify equity beta, but only if it persists when stress rises.
asset-vs-spy.example: TLT may offset SPY in a growth shock but fail during an inflation shock.

asset-corr-change.title: 20-day change in relationship
asset-corr-change.measure: Whether the asset is becoming more or less connected to the rest of the universe.
asset-corr-change.current: Positive values mean dependence has increased during the last 20 sessions.
asset-corr-change.history: A rapid increase is often more informative than a stable high level.
asset-corr-change.effect: Supports or weakens the current fragility warning.
asset-corr-change.portfolio: A previously independent hedge becoming highly correlated can leave the portfolio unexpectedly exposed.
asset-corr-change.example: Gold can stop diversifying if dollar or real-yield stress starts controlling both gold and equities.

driver-overview.title: Model driver contributions
driver-overview.measure: Which variables are currently pushing the rally or crash score higher or lower.
driver-overview.current: Red positive values increase that score; green negative values reduce it.
driver-overview.history: The numbers are relative contributions on the ORCA-Lite scale, not probabilities.
driver-overview.effect: Explains the current ranking but does not prove the variable caused the market move.
driver-overview.portfolio: Use the driver mix to distinguish structural risk from an oversold or volatility-driven signal.
driver-overview.example: A crash warning driven by rising network density is different from one driven only by a one-day volatility spike.

driver-spectral-share.title: Spectral / graph share
driver-spectral-share.technical: Share of absolute model contribution from correlation-network features
driver-spectral-share.measure: How much of the score explanation comes from eigenvalue, correlation, and graph-topology features rather than price indicators.
driver-spectral-share.history: The ORCA paper emphasises structural features for crash detection.
driver-spectral-share.effect: A high share means the warning is mainly about market structure.
driver-spectral-share.portfolio: Structural warnings may appear before headline volatility fully reacts.
driver-spectral-share.example: The crash score rises because diversification is collapsing even while the index remains near its high.

outcome-performance.title: Performance by regime
outcome-performance.technical: Event-based forward return and drawdown analysis
outcome-performance.measure: What the selected index did after the first day of each historical regime episode.
outcome-performance.current: The table summarises 10-day outcomes for the selected index and time window.
outcome-performance.history: Episodes—not every daily observation—are counted to reduce repeated labels from the same event.
outcome-performance.effect: This is a validation tool, not an input to the current signal.
outcome-performance.portfolio: A useful regime should show economically different forward outcomes after costs and without look-ahead leakage.
outcome-performance.example: If Crisis episodes do not have worse forward drawdowns than Normal episodes, the regime map has little practical value.

crash-0.title: 20-day realised volatility
crash-0.measure: The annualised variability of daily SPY returns over the last 20 trading days.
crash-0.history: The feature ranks at the 11.7th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-0.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.115 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-0.portfolio: It can confirm stress, but it often reacts after fragility has already increased.
crash-0.example: Higher realised volatility means the market is making larger daily moves than usual.

crash-1.title: Clustering coefficient
crash-1.measure: How often strongly linked assets form tightly connected groups or triangles.
crash-1.history: The feature ranks at the 73.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-1.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.046 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-1.portfolio: Dense clusters can reveal duplicate exposures that look diversified only because they use different tickers.
crash-1.example: If SPY links to QQQ and XLK, and QQQ also links to XLK, they form a tight cluster.

crash-2.title: Price versus 50-day moving average
crash-2.measure: The percentage distance between SPY and its 50-day average price.
crash-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-2.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.044 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-2.portfolio: Below-trend prices can confirm weakness or create rebound potential depending on the wider regime.
crash-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

crash-3.title: 60-day drawdown
crash-3.measure: How far SPY is below its highest close in the last 60 trading days.
crash-3.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-3.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.040 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-3.portfolio: A deep drawdown can create rebound potential while also indicating an unstable market.
crash-3.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

crash-4.title: One-factor absorption ratio (AR1)
crash-4.measure: The share of total cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
crash-4.history: The feature ranks at the 47.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-4.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.010 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-4.portfolio: A high or rapidly rising value means diversification is becoming more dependent on one macro driver.
crash-4.example: If AR1 is 40%, one broad force—such as liquidity, rates, inflation, or fear—explains about 40% of the movement across all 24 assets.

crash-5.title: Effective rank / effective bets
crash-5.measure: An estimate of how many statistically independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
crash-5.history: The feature ranks at the 49.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-5.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.002 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-5.portfolio: A falling value warns that the number of holdings may overstate actual diversification.
crash-5.example: A reading of 8 means 24 tickers currently behave more like eight genuinely different bets.

crash-6.title: Strong-connection share (edge density)
crash-6.measure: The fraction of all 276 unique asset pairs with absolute correlation above 0.50.
crash-6.history: The feature ranks at the 50.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-6.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.000 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-6.portfolio: A high or rising value means shocks can spread across more of the portfolio.
crash-6.example: A reading of 46% means roughly 127 of 276 pairs have a strong relationship.

rally-0.title: Five-day return / short-term reversal
rally-0.measure: SPY's total return over the last five trading days.
rally-0.history: The feature ranks at the 20.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-0.effect: It currently reduces the rally score by -0.120 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-0.portfolio: The signal is more credible when breadth and credit also improve.
rally-0.example: A positive rebound after a drawdown may strengthen a rally setup.

rally-1.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-1.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.100 on the ORCA-Lite scale.

rally-1.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

rally-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-2.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.088 on the ORCA-Lite scale.

rally-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

rally-3.title: 20-day realised volatility

rally-3.history: The feature ranks at the 14.7th percentile in its comparison history.

rally-4.title: 20-day drawdown

rally-4.portfolio: A deep reading can raise mean-reversion potential, but should be read with crash risk.
rally-4.example: It measures shorter-horizon damage and oversold conditions.

rally-5.title: Cross-asset breadth

structure-overview.title: Structural health
structure-overview.measure: Whether the 24 instruments are still behaving like genuinely different investments, or are being controlled by the same macro force.
structure-overview.current: The current EWM · 30D half-life view is summarised by four plain-language cards.
structure-overview.effect: Raises or lowers the fragility warning, but does not by itself forecast a market decline.
structure-overview.portfolio: Treat the book as more concentrated than the ticker count suggests when several measures deteriorate together.
structure-overview.example: Owning SPY, QQQ, XLK, XLY, EFA, and HYG can look like six positions but behave like one broad risk-on trade.

struct-ar1.title: One factor controls the market
struct-ar1.technical: Absorption ratio AR1 / first eigenvalue share
struct-ar1.measure: The share of all cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
struct-ar1.current: 45.2% of total movement is explained by one factor.
struct-ar1.effect: A rising reading increases fragility because more assets answer to the same market “conductor.”
struct-ar1.portfolio: Expect diversification to work less well if a shock hits the dominant factor.
struct-ar1.example: During a liquidity shock, technology, banks, small caps, high yield, and overseas equities may all become the same trade.

struct-erank.title: 24 assets behave like fewer bets
struct-erank.measure: An estimate of how many independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
struct-erank.effect: A falling effective rank raises structural risk.
struct-erank.portfolio: Position count may overstate diversification. Size the book as if it contained roughly this number of independent bets.
struct-erank.example: SPY, QQQ, XLK, and XLY may all belong to one US growth cluster rather than four separate ideas.

struct-links.title: Strongly connected asset pairs
struct-links.measure: How many of the 276 unique asset pairs have a correlation strong enough to pass the selected threshold.
struct-links.current: 184 of 276 pairs are currently classified as strong links.
struct-links.history: That equals 67% of all possible pairs.
struct-links.effect: More links mean a shock can travel through more parts of the portfolio.
struct-links.portfolio: Look for duplicate exposures and avoid assuming that different tickers imply different risk.
struct-links.example: If SPY–QQQ, QQQ–XLK, and SPY–XLK are all strong links, the three form one crowded cluster.

struct-speed.title: Speed of deterioration
struct-speed.measure: How quickly the share of strong cross-asset relationships is changing.
struct-speed.current: Strong-link density changed +2.9 percentage points in 20 trading days.
struct-speed.history: The speed of change can be more informative than a permanently high but stable level.
struct-speed.effect: Rapid deterioration strengthens the warning because the market structure is changing now.
struct-speed.portfolio: Raise monitoring frequency and reduce marginal risk before the headline index necessarily breaks.
struct-speed.example: A market can remain near its high while correlations underneath the surface rise sharply.

advanced-ar3.title: Top three factors share
advanced-ar3.measure: The percentage of total cross-asset movement explained by the three largest common factors.
advanced-ar3.current: The top three factors explain 68.3% of movement.
advanced-ar3.effect: Raises structural concentration when it climbs.
advanced-ar3.portfolio: A portfolio may be exposed mainly to three macro drivers such as risk appetite, rates, and the US dollar.
advanced-ar3.example: Twenty-four assets can still be mostly controlled by only three broad forces.

advanced-gap.title: Dominant factor ratio
advanced-gap.technical: Spectral gap: first eigenvalue divided by second eigenvalue
advanced-gap.measure: How much stronger the largest common factor is than the second-largest factor.
advanced-gap.current: The first factor is approximately 2.8× as strong as the second.
advanced-gap.effect: Supports a herding or one-factor-market warning.
advanced-gap.portfolio: If the dominant factor reverses, many apparently unrelated positions can move together.
advanced-gap.example: A single “rates higher” trade can dominate utilities, REITs, technology, bonds, and the dollar.

advanced-cluster.title: Cluster tightness
advanced-cluster.measure: How often strongly linked assets form closed groups in which each member is connected to the others.
advanced-cluster.effect: Can raise crash risk when crowded groups become tightly synchronized.
advanced-cluster.portfolio: A cluster can amplify contagion because weakness in one member is confirmed by the others.
advanced-cluster.example: SPY, QQQ, and XLK all strongly linked to one another form a closed triangle.

advanced-condition.title: Matrix instability
advanced-condition.technical: Condition number of the correlation matrix
advanced-condition.measure: How unbalanced the correlation matrix is between its strongest and weakest risk directions.
advanced-condition.effect: Raises concern about fragile covariance estimates rather than directly forecasting price direction.
advanced-condition.portfolio: Do not trust precise optimizer weights when the matrix is unstable; use constraints and robustness checks.
advanced-condition.example: Like a table carrying most of its weight on one leg, a small disturbance can change the balance.

advanced-mp.title: Common factor above random noise
advanced-mp.measure: Whether the dominant eigenvalue is larger than what random statistical noise could plausibly generate.
advanced-mp.current: The excess is 9.1 above the random-noise boundary.
advanced-mp.effect: Confirms whether the common market structure is likely real rather than accidental correlation.
advanced-mp.portfolio: Treat the dominant factor as economically meaningful while still testing stability out of sample.
advanced-mp.example: It asks whether the “one market conductor” is real or just a pattern created by chance.

asset-avg-relationship.title: Average relationship
asset-avg-relationship.measure: The average strength of one asset’s relationship with the other 23 assets. Positive and negative signs are both counted as strong dependence.
asset-avg-relationship.current: The table shows the raw value and a Low / Medium / High label.
asset-avg-relationship.history: A rising average means the asset is becoming less independent.
asset-avg-relationship.effect: This is a dependence measure, not a buy or sell signal.
asset-avg-relationship.portfolio: High average relationship means the asset may duplicate risks already present elsewhere in the book.
asset-avg-relationship.example: An average of 0.56 means the asset is fairly connected to the broader universe.

asset-strong-links.title: Strong links
asset-strong-links.technical: Network degree at the selected threshold
asset-strong-links.measure: The number of other assets whose correlation passes 0.30 under the current edge setting.
asset-strong-links.current: The table reports a count out of 23 possible relationships.
asset-strong-links.history: A rising count means the asset is moving toward the centre of the market network.
asset-strong-links.effect: High connectivity can confirm broad contagion or duplicate beta.
asset-strong-links.portfolio: Owning multiple highly connected hubs may not add diversification.
asset-strong-links.example: 18 / 23 means the asset has strong relationships with eighteen other instruments.

asset-strongest-link.title: Strongest relationship
asset-strongest-link.measure: The single asset with the strongest current relationship to the selected ticker.
asset-strongest-link.current: The sign is retained: positive means they move together; negative means they tend to move opposite.
asset-strongest-link.history: Relationships can change across macro regimes.
asset-strongest-link.effect: Useful for identifying duplicate exposure or a possible offset.
asset-strongest-link.portfolio: Validate whether the relationship is stable before treating it as a hedge.
asset-strongest-link.example: QQQ +0.85 with XLK suggests the two positions may duplicate US growth risk.

asset-vs-spy.title: Relationship to SPY
asset-vs-spy.measure: How closely the asset currently moves with the broad US equity market.
asset-vs-spy.current: Positive values imply equity-like co-movement; negative values may indicate an offset.
asset-vs-spy.history: The sign and magnitude can change between growth, inflation, and liquidity shocks.
asset-vs-spy.effect: Helps classify the asset’s current portfolio role.
asset-vs-spy.portfolio: A low or negative SPY correlation can diversify equity beta, but only if it persists when stress rises.
asset-vs-spy.example: TLT may offset SPY in a growth shock but fail during an inflation shock.

asset-corr-change.title: 20-day change in relationship
asset-corr-change.measure: Whether the asset is becoming more or less connected to the rest of the universe.
asset-corr-change.current: Positive values mean dependence has increased during the last 20 sessions.
asset-corr-change.history: A rapid increase is often more informative than a stable high level.
asset-corr-change.effect: Supports or weakens the current fragility warning.
asset-corr-change.portfolio: A previously independent hedge becoming highly correlated can leave the portfolio unexpectedly exposed.
asset-corr-change.example: Gold can stop diversifying if dollar or real-yield stress starts controlling both gold and equities.

driver-overview.title: Model driver contributions
driver-overview.measure: Which variables are currently pushing the rally or crash score higher or lower.
driver-overview.current: Red positive values increase that score; green negative values reduce it.
driver-overview.history: The numbers are relative contributions on the ORCA-Lite scale, not probabilities.
driver-overview.effect: Explains the current ranking but does not prove the variable caused the market move.
driver-overview.portfolio: Use the driver mix to distinguish structural risk from an oversold or volatility-driven signal.
driver-overview.example: A crash warning driven by rising network density is different from one driven only by a one-day volatility spike.

driver-spectral-share.title: Spectral / graph share
driver-spectral-share.technical: Share of absolute model contribution from correlation-network features
driver-spectral-share.measure: How much of the score explanation comes from eigenvalue, correlation, and graph-topology features rather than price indicators.
driver-spectral-share.history: The ORCA paper emphasises structural features for crash detection.
driver-spectral-share.effect: A high share means the warning is mainly about market structure.
driver-spectral-share.portfolio: Structural warnings may appear before headline volatility fully reacts.
driver-spectral-share.example: The crash score rises because diversification is collapsing even while the index remains near its high.

outcome-performance.title: Performance by regime
outcome-performance.technical: Event-based forward return and drawdown analysis
outcome-performance.measure: What the selected index did after the first day of each historical regime episode.
outcome-performance.current: The table summarises 10-day outcomes for the selected index and time window.
outcome-performance.history: Episodes—not every daily observation—are counted to reduce repeated labels from the same event.
outcome-performance.effect: This is a validation tool, not an input to the current signal.
outcome-performance.portfolio: A useful regime should show economically different forward outcomes after costs and without look-ahead leakage.
outcome-performance.example: If Crisis episodes do not have worse forward drawdowns than Normal episodes, the regime map has little practical value.

crash-0.title: 20-day realised volatility
crash-0.measure: The annualised variability of daily SPY returns over the last 20 trading days.
crash-0.history: The feature ranks at the 11.7th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-0.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.115 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-0.portfolio: It can confirm stress, but it often reacts after fragility has already increased.
crash-0.example: Higher realised volatility means the market is making larger daily moves than usual.

crash-1.title: Clustering coefficient
crash-1.measure: How often strongly linked assets form tightly connected groups or triangles.
crash-1.history: The feature ranks at the 73.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-1.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.046 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-1.portfolio: Dense clusters can reveal duplicate exposures that look diversified only because they use different tickers.
crash-1.example: If SPY links to QQQ and XLK, and QQQ also links to XLK, they form a tight cluster.

crash-2.title: Price versus 50-day moving average
crash-2.measure: The percentage distance between SPY and its 50-day average price.
crash-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-2.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.044 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-2.portfolio: Below-trend prices can confirm weakness or create rebound potential depending on the wider regime.
crash-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

crash-3.title: 60-day drawdown
crash-3.measure: How far SPY is below its highest close in the last 60 trading days.
crash-3.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-3.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.040 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-3.portfolio: A deep drawdown can create rebound potential while also indicating an unstable market.
crash-3.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

crash-4.title: One-factor absorption ratio (AR1)
crash-4.measure: The share of total cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
crash-4.history: The feature ranks at the 47.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-4.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.010 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-4.portfolio: A high or rapidly rising value means diversification is becoming more dependent on one macro driver.
crash-4.example: If AR1 is 40%, one broad force—such as liquidity, rates, inflation, or fear—explains about 40% of the movement across all 24 assets.

crash-5.title: Effective rank / effective bets
crash-5.measure: An estimate of how many statistically independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
crash-5.history: The feature ranks at the 49.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-5.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.002 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-5.portfolio: A falling value warns that the number of holdings may overstate actual diversification.
crash-5.example: A reading of 8 means 24 tickers currently behave more like eight genuinely different bets.

crash-6.title: Strong-connection share (edge density)
crash-6.measure: The fraction of all 276 unique asset pairs with absolute correlation above 0.50.
crash-6.history: The feature ranks at the 50.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-6.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.000 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-6.portfolio: A high or rising value means shocks can spread across more of the portfolio.
crash-6.example: A reading of 46% means roughly 127 of 276 pairs have a strong relationship.

rally-0.title: Five-day return / short-term reversal
rally-0.measure: SPY's total return over the last five trading days.
rally-0.history: The feature ranks at the 20.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-0.effect: It currently reduces the rally score by -0.120 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-0.portfolio: The signal is more credible when breadth and credit also improve.
rally-0.example: A positive rebound after a drawdown may strengthen a rally setup.

rally-1.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-1.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.100 on the ORCA-Lite scale.

rally-1.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

rally-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-2.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.088 on the ORCA-Lite scale.

rally-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

rally-3.title: 20-day realised volatility

rally-3.history: The feature ranks at the 14.7th percentile in its comparison history.

rally-4.title: 20-day drawdown

rally-4.portfolio: A deep reading can raise mean-reversion potential, but should be read with crash risk.
rally-4.example: It measures shorter-horizon damage and oversold conditions.

rally-5.title: Cross-asset breadth

structure-overview.title: Structural health
structure-overview.measure: Whether the 24 instruments are still behaving like genuinely different investments, or are being controlled by the same macro force.
structure-overview.current: The current EWM · 30D half-life view is summarised by four plain-language cards.
structure-overview.effect: Raises or lowers the fragility warning, but does not by itself forecast a market decline.
structure-overview.portfolio: Treat the book as more concentrated than the ticker count suggests when several measures deteriorate together.
structure-overview.example: Owning SPY, QQQ, XLK, XLY, EFA, and HYG can look like six positions but behave like one broad risk-on trade.

struct-ar1.title: One factor controls the market
struct-ar1.technical: Absorption ratio AR1 / first eigenvalue share
struct-ar1.measure: The share of all cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
struct-ar1.current: 45.2% of total movement is explained by one factor.
struct-ar1.effect: A rising reading increases fragility because more assets answer to the same market “conductor.”
struct-ar1.portfolio: Expect diversification to work less well if a shock hits the dominant factor.
struct-ar1.example: During a liquidity shock, technology, banks, small caps, high yield, and overseas equities may all become the same trade.

struct-erank.title: 24 assets behave like fewer bets
struct-erank.measure: An estimate of how many independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
struct-erank.effect: A falling effective rank raises structural risk.
struct-erank.portfolio: Position count may overstate diversification. Size the book as if it contained roughly this number of independent bets.
struct-erank.example: SPY, QQQ, XLK, and XLY may all belong to one US growth cluster rather than four separate ideas.

struct-links.title: Strongly connected asset pairs
struct-links.measure: How many of the 276 unique asset pairs have a correlation strong enough to pass the selected threshold.
struct-links.current: 88 of 276 pairs are currently classified as strong links.
struct-links.history: That equals 32% of all possible pairs.
struct-links.effect: More links mean a shock can travel through more parts of the portfolio.
struct-links.portfolio: Look for duplicate exposures and avoid assuming that different tickers imply different risk.
struct-links.example: If SPY–QQQ, QQQ–XLK, and SPY–XLK are all strong links, the three form one crowded cluster.

struct-speed.title: Speed of deterioration
struct-speed.measure: How quickly the share of strong cross-asset relationships is changing.
struct-speed.current: Strong-link density changed -0.7 percentage points in 20 trading days.
struct-speed.history: The speed of change can be more informative than a permanently high but stable level.
struct-speed.effect: Rapid deterioration strengthens the warning because the market structure is changing now.
struct-speed.portfolio: Raise monitoring frequency and reduce marginal risk before the headline index necessarily breaks.
struct-speed.example: A market can remain near its high while correlations underneath the surface rise sharply.

advanced-ar3.title: Top three factors share
advanced-ar3.measure: The percentage of total cross-asset movement explained by the three largest common factors.
advanced-ar3.current: The top three factors explain 68.3% of movement.
advanced-ar3.effect: Raises structural concentration when it climbs.
advanced-ar3.portfolio: A portfolio may be exposed mainly to three macro drivers such as risk appetite, rates, and the US dollar.
advanced-ar3.example: Twenty-four assets can still be mostly controlled by only three broad forces.

advanced-gap.title: Dominant factor ratio
advanced-gap.technical: Spectral gap: first eigenvalue divided by second eigenvalue
advanced-gap.measure: How much stronger the largest common factor is than the second-largest factor.
advanced-gap.current: The first factor is approximately 2.8× as strong as the second.
advanced-gap.effect: Supports a herding or one-factor-market warning.
advanced-gap.portfolio: If the dominant factor reverses, many apparently unrelated positions can move together.
advanced-gap.example: A single “rates higher” trade can dominate utilities, REITs, technology, bonds, and the dollar.

advanced-cluster.title: Cluster tightness
advanced-cluster.measure: How often strongly linked assets form closed groups in which each member is connected to the others.
advanced-cluster.effect: Can raise crash risk when crowded groups become tightly synchronized.
advanced-cluster.portfolio: A cluster can amplify contagion because weakness in one member is confirmed by the others.
advanced-cluster.example: SPY, QQQ, and XLK all strongly linked to one another form a closed triangle.

advanced-condition.title: Matrix instability
advanced-condition.technical: Condition number of the correlation matrix
advanced-condition.measure: How unbalanced the correlation matrix is between its strongest and weakest risk directions.
advanced-condition.effect: Raises concern about fragile covariance estimates rather than directly forecasting price direction.
advanced-condition.portfolio: Do not trust precise optimizer weights when the matrix is unstable; use constraints and robustness checks.
advanced-condition.example: Like a table carrying most of its weight on one leg, a small disturbance can change the balance.

advanced-mp.title: Common factor above random noise
advanced-mp.measure: Whether the dominant eigenvalue is larger than what random statistical noise could plausibly generate.
advanced-mp.current: The excess is 9.1 above the random-noise boundary.
advanced-mp.effect: Confirms whether the common market structure is likely real rather than accidental correlation.
advanced-mp.portfolio: Treat the dominant factor as economically meaningful while still testing stability out of sample.
advanced-mp.example: It asks whether the “one market conductor” is real or just a pattern created by chance.

asset-avg-relationship.title: Average relationship
asset-avg-relationship.measure: The average strength of one asset’s relationship with the other 23 assets. Positive and negative signs are both counted as strong dependence.
asset-avg-relationship.current: The table shows the raw value and a Low / Medium / High label.
asset-avg-relationship.history: A rising average means the asset is becoming less independent.
asset-avg-relationship.effect: This is a dependence measure, not a buy or sell signal.
asset-avg-relationship.portfolio: High average relationship means the asset may duplicate risks already present elsewhere in the book.
asset-avg-relationship.example: An average of 0.56 means the asset is fairly connected to the broader universe.

asset-strong-links.title: Strong links
asset-strong-links.technical: Network degree at the selected threshold
asset-strong-links.measure: The number of other assets whose correlation passes 0.50 under the current edge setting.
asset-strong-links.current: The table reports a count out of 23 possible relationships.
asset-strong-links.history: A rising count means the asset is moving toward the centre of the market network.
asset-strong-links.effect: High connectivity can confirm broad contagion or duplicate beta.
asset-strong-links.portfolio: Owning multiple highly connected hubs may not add diversification.
asset-strong-links.example: 18 / 23 means the asset has strong relationships with eighteen other instruments.

asset-strongest-link.title: Strongest relationship
asset-strongest-link.measure: The single asset with the strongest current relationship to the selected ticker.
asset-strongest-link.current: The sign is retained: positive means they move together; negative means they tend to move opposite.
asset-strongest-link.history: Relationships can change across macro regimes.
asset-strongest-link.effect: Useful for identifying duplicate exposure or a possible offset.
asset-strongest-link.portfolio: Validate whether the relationship is stable before treating it as a hedge.
asset-strongest-link.example: QQQ +0.85 with XLK suggests the two positions may duplicate US growth risk.

asset-vs-spy.title: Relationship to SPY
asset-vs-spy.measure: How closely the asset currently moves with the broad US equity market.
asset-vs-spy.current: Positive values imply equity-like co-movement; negative values may indicate an offset.
asset-vs-spy.history: The sign and magnitude can change between growth, inflation, and liquidity shocks.
asset-vs-spy.effect: Helps classify the asset’s current portfolio role.
asset-vs-spy.portfolio: A low or negative SPY correlation can diversify equity beta, but only if it persists when stress rises.
asset-vs-spy.example: TLT may offset SPY in a growth shock but fail during an inflation shock.

asset-corr-change.title: 20-day change in relationship
asset-corr-change.measure: Whether the asset is becoming more or less connected to the rest of the universe.
asset-corr-change.current: Positive values mean dependence has increased during the last 20 sessions.
asset-corr-change.history: A rapid increase is often more informative than a stable high level.
asset-corr-change.effect: Supports or weakens the current fragility warning.
asset-corr-change.portfolio: A previously independent hedge becoming highly correlated can leave the portfolio unexpectedly exposed.
asset-corr-change.example: Gold can stop diversifying if dollar or real-yield stress starts controlling both gold and equities.

driver-overview.title: Model driver contributions
driver-overview.measure: Which variables are currently pushing the rally or crash score higher or lower.
driver-overview.current: Red positive values increase that score; green negative values reduce it.
driver-overview.history: The numbers are relative contributions on the ORCA-Lite scale, not probabilities.
driver-overview.effect: Explains the current ranking but does not prove the variable caused the market move.
driver-overview.portfolio: Use the driver mix to distinguish structural risk from an oversold or volatility-driven signal.
driver-overview.example: A crash warning driven by rising network density is different from one driven only by a one-day volatility spike.

driver-spectral-share.title: Spectral / graph share
driver-spectral-share.technical: Share of absolute model contribution from correlation-network features
driver-spectral-share.measure: How much of the score explanation comes from eigenvalue, correlation, and graph-topology features rather than price indicators.
driver-spectral-share.history: The ORCA paper emphasises structural features for crash detection.
driver-spectral-share.effect: A high share means the warning is mainly about market structure.
driver-spectral-share.portfolio: Structural warnings may appear before headline volatility fully reacts.
driver-spectral-share.example: The crash score rises because diversification is collapsing even while the index remains near its high.

outcome-performance.title: Performance by regime
outcome-performance.technical: Event-based forward return and drawdown analysis
outcome-performance.measure: What the selected index did after the first day of each historical regime episode.
outcome-performance.current: The table summarises 10-day outcomes for the selected index and time window.
outcome-performance.history: Episodes—not every daily observation—are counted to reduce repeated labels from the same event.
outcome-performance.effect: This is a validation tool, not an input to the current signal.
outcome-performance.portfolio: A useful regime should show economically different forward outcomes after costs and without look-ahead leakage.
outcome-performance.example: If Crisis episodes do not have worse forward drawdowns than Normal episodes, the regime map has little practical value.

crash-0.title: 20-day realised volatility
crash-0.measure: The annualised variability of daily SPY returns over the last 20 trading days.
crash-0.history: The feature ranks at the 11.7th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-0.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.115 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-0.portfolio: It can confirm stress, but it often reacts after fragility has already increased.
crash-0.example: Higher realised volatility means the market is making larger daily moves than usual.

crash-1.title: Clustering coefficient
crash-1.measure: How often strongly linked assets form tightly connected groups or triangles.
crash-1.history: The feature ranks at the 73.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-1.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.046 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-1.portfolio: Dense clusters can reveal duplicate exposures that look diversified only because they use different tickers.
crash-1.example: If SPY links to QQQ and XLK, and QQQ also links to XLK, they form a tight cluster.

crash-2.title: Price versus 50-day moving average
crash-2.measure: The percentage distance between SPY and its 50-day average price.
crash-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-2.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.044 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-2.portfolio: Below-trend prices can confirm weakness or create rebound potential depending on the wider regime.
crash-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

crash-3.title: 60-day drawdown
crash-3.measure: How far SPY is below its highest close in the last 60 trading days.
crash-3.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-3.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.040 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-3.portfolio: A deep drawdown can create rebound potential while also indicating an unstable market.
crash-3.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

crash-4.title: One-factor absorption ratio (AR1)
crash-4.measure: The share of total cross-asset movement explained by the single largest common factor.
crash-4.history: The feature ranks at the 47.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-4.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.010 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-4.portfolio: A high or rapidly rising value means diversification is becoming more dependent on one macro driver.
crash-4.example: If AR1 is 40%, one broad force—such as liquidity, rates, inflation, or fear—explains about 40% of the movement across all 24 assets.

crash-5.title: Effective rank / effective bets
crash-5.measure: An estimate of how many statistically independent sources of risk remain in the 24-asset universe.
crash-5.history: The feature ranks at the 49.4th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-5.effect: It currently reduces the crash score by -0.002 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-5.portfolio: A falling value warns that the number of holdings may overstate actual diversification.
crash-5.example: A reading of 8 means 24 tickers currently behave more like eight genuinely different bets.

crash-6.title: Strong-connection share (edge density)
crash-6.measure: The fraction of all 276 unique asset pairs with absolute correlation above 0.50.
crash-6.history: The feature ranks at the 50.0th percentile in its comparison history.
crash-6.effect: It currently raises the crash score by +0.000 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
crash-6.portfolio: A high or rising value means shocks can spread across more of the portfolio.
crash-6.example: A reading of 46% means roughly 127 of 276 pairs have a strong relationship.

rally-0.title: Five-day return / short-term reversal
rally-0.measure: SPY's total return over the last five trading days.
rally-0.history: The feature ranks at the 20.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-0.effect: It currently reduces the rally score by -0.120 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-0.portfolio: The signal is more credible when breadth and credit also improve.
rally-0.example: A positive rebound after a drawdown may strengthen a rally setup.

rally-1.title: 60-day drawdown
rally-1.measure: How far SPY is below its highest close in the last 60 trading days.
rally-1.history: The feature ranks at the 70.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-1.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.100 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-1.portfolio: A deep drawdown can create rebound potential while also indicating an unstable market.
rally-1.example: A -10% reading means SPY is 10% below its two-to-three-month high.

rally-2.history: The feature ranks at the 72.0th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-2.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.088 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-2.portfolio: Below-trend prices can confirm weakness or create rebound potential depending on the wider regime.
rally-2.example: A -5% reading means SPY trades 5% below its medium-term trend.

rally-3.title: 20-day realised volatility

rally-3.history: The feature ranks at the 14.7th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-3.effect: It currently reduces the rally score by -0.070 on the ORCA-Lite scale.

rally-3.example: Higher realised volatility means the market is making larger daily moves than usual.

rally-4.title: 20-day drawdown
rally-4.measure: How far SPY is below its highest close in the last 20 trading days.
rally-4.history: The feature ranks at the 69.6th percentile in its comparison history.
rally-4.effect: It currently raises the rally score by +0.059 on the ORCA-Lite scale.
rally-4.portfolio: A deep reading can raise mean-reversion potential, but should be read with crash risk.
rally-4.example: It measures shorter-horizon damage and oversold conditions.

rally-5.title: Cross-asset breadth
rally-5.measure: The share of the 24 assets trading above their own 20-day moving averages.
rally-5.history: The feature ranks at the 54.0th percentile in its comparison history.
